J U D G M E N T
PER HON’BLE MR. VIRENDER BHAT, JUDICIAL MEMBER
1. The Appellants have, in this appeal, assailed the order dated
3rd October, 2022 passed by the 3rd Respondent – Uttar Pradesh
Electricity Regulatory Commission (hereinafter referred to as “the
Commission”) in Petition No. 1824 of 2022 filed by 1st Respondent.
2. The Appellant No. 1 is a deemed licensee under Section 14 of
the Electricity Act, 2003 and is functioning as distribution, retail and
bulk supply licensee under UP Electricity Reforms Act, 1999
(Reforms Act). The Appellant Nos. 2 to 6 are distribution licensees in
the State of UP in terms of Section 2(17) of Electricity Act, 2003.
However in the context of the present Appeal, the Appellant Nos. 2 to
6 are Long Term Transmission Customers (LTTCs) of the 1st
Respondent – Obra C – Badaun Transmission Limited (in short
“OBTL”).
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 452 of 2022 Page 3 of 34

3. The 1st Respondent (also referred to as OBTL) is an intra-state
transmission licensee in the State of UP and was entrusted to
implement as well as operate “Evacuation of power from Obra-C
(2x660 MW) Thermal Power Project and Construction of 400 KV GIS
sub-station, Badaun with associated transmission lines” hereinafter
referred to as “the project” on Build, Own, Operate & Maintain basis
under TBCB mode, for which Transmission Service Agreement (TSA)
dated 15th October, 2018 was entered between the 1st Respondent
and LTTCs. A supplementary TSA dated 15.10.2020 was also signed
between 1st Respondent and LTTCs along with 2nd Respondent -
UPPTCL in which UPPTCL was nominated by LTTCs to act as their
nominee while indemnifying UPPTCL from any claim.
4. The Schedule Commercial Operation Date (SCOD) of the
project as per Schedule -3 of TSA for LOT-1 was 21st November,
2020, for LOT-II was 1st February, 2021.
5. It appears that the implementation of the project was delayed
on account of various Force Majeure events as contended by the 1st
Respondent. Accordingly, various notices were addressed in this
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 452 of 2022 Page 4 of 34

regard by the 1st Respondent to the LTTCs informing them about the
Force Majeure events, the details of which are as under :-
(a) Stoppage of construction due to flooding of
construction sites (Notice dated 28.09.2019 &
15.10.2019)
(b) Delay in grant of transmission license/ in adoption of
Tariff in grant of authorisation under Section 164 of
the Act (Notice dated 18.10.2019)
(c) Cessation of force majeure event of flooding of
location and approach due to heavy monsoon
(Notice dated 11.11.2019)
(d) ROW issues due to delays in receiving authorisation
under Section 164 of the Act (Notice dated
14.11.2019)
(e) Sudden strike called by employees of UPPCL
(Notice dated 28.11.2019)
(f) Imposition of Section 144 due to protests against
Citizenship Amendment Act (Notice dated
23.12.2019 & 10.01.2020)
(g) Delay in receipt of materials due to closing
enterprises in China because of Covid-19 pandemic
(Notice dated 20.02.2020)
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 452 of 2022 Page 5 of 34

(h) Imposition of lockdown and restriction imposed by
Government of Uttar Pradesh due to Covid-19
pandemic (Notice dated 23.03.2020)
(i) Imposition of countrywide lockdown due to Covid-19
pandemic (Notice dated 26.03.2020)
(j) Extension of countrywide lockdown due to Covid-19
pandemic (Notice dated 15.04.2020, 04.05.2020 &
18.05.2020)
(k) Restrictions and lockdown imposed due to Covid-19
pandemic (Notice dated 06.06.2020, 04.07.2020,
20.08.2020, 14.09.2020 & 23.10.2020)
(l) Lockdown imposed due to Covid-10 Pandemic
(Notice dated 29.04.2021)
6. Subsequently, while letters dated 23rd March, 2021 and 2nd
April, 2021, the 1st Respondent intimated the LTTCs about the
deemed COD of Element 1 and Elements 2 to 8 of LOT-1 as 30th
March, 2021 and 9th April, 2021 respectively. The 1st Respondent also
claimed entitlement of transmission charges from these dates.
Thereafter, the 1st Respondent started raising monthly transmission
charges invoices for both Element I as well Elements 2 to 8 of LOT I
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 452 of 2022 Page 6 of 34

of the project from the date of said deemed COD along with
supplementary bills towards late payment surcharge.
7. Vide letter dated 1st December, 2021, Appellant No. 4 – PVVNL
informed 1st Respondent that it has considered the deemed COD of
Element I and Elements 2 to 8 of LOT-I as 30th April, 2021 and 16th
April, 2021 respectively, which was disputed by the 1st Respondent
vide the reply dated 1st December, 2021.
8. At the same time, Appellant No. 1 – UPPCL vide letter dated
7th December, 2021, raised invoices verification statement of
Rs.8,61,37,692/- as recoverable amount towards liquidated damages
for delay of 38 days and 53 days in achieving deemed COD of these
elements i.e. Element I and Elements 2 to 8 of LOT-I respectively.
Vide reply dated 15th December, 2021, 1st Respondent stated that it
was entitled to extension of SCOD of LOT-I on account of Force
Majeure events as per Article 4 and 4.1 & 2 of TSA as well as on the
basis of notifications dated 27th July, 2020 and 12th June, 2021 issued
by Ministry of Power, Govt. of India on account of Covid-19 Pandemic
and nationwide lockdown thereby granting extension of 5 months and
3 months respectively to the SCOD of all transmission projects.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 452 of 2022 Page 7 of 34

9. In these circumstances, the 1st Respondent had approached
the Commission with petition No. 1824 of 2022 claiming extension of
SCOD for LOT-I elements of its project i.e. Element Nos. 1 to 8 by a
period of 8 months and a declaration that Appellant No. 1 is not
entitled to levy liquidated damages for any delay in commissioning of
these elements. Following Force Majeure events were agitated by the
1st Respondent in this petition:-
“A. Heavy rainfall leading to flooding of pits excavated
for laying down foundation of transmission towers.
B. Delay in grant of Transmission License by the Ld.
UPERC.
C. Delay in adoption of tariff by the Ld. UPERC.
D. COVID-19 pandemic.
E. Delay in grant of authorization under Section 164
[Exercise of powers of Telegraph Authority in certain
cases] of the Act.
F. Strike called by employees of UPPCL.
G. Public protests against the Citizenship Amendment
Bill.
10. The petition was disposed of by the Commission vide
impugned order dated 3rd October, 2022 thereby rejecting the claim
of the 1st Respondent with regards to all the Force Majeure events
except Covid-19 Pandemic. Accordingly, the Appellants are
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 452 of 2022 Page 8 of 34

aggrieved by the impugned order of the Commission in so far as it
has upheld the claim of Respondent No. 1 for extension of COD of
Element I till its deemed COD accepted by LTTCs i.e. 30th April, 2021
and that of the Elements 2 to 8 till their deemed COD accepted by
LTTCs i.e. 16th April, 2021 considering the Covid-19 Pandemic as the
Force Majeure events affecting the completion of the project.
11. Thus, the only issue involved in the appeal for our consideration
is :-
“Whether the Covid-19 Pandemic and subsequent
lockdown imposed by the Government of India constituted
a Force Majeure event in terms of the provisions of the
TSA executed between the parties entitling the 1st
Respondent to extension of SCOD of the project”.
12. According to the Appellants, the impugned order warrants
interference by this Tribunal in this appeal on account of the
following:-
“A. The conclusion that OBTL has been affected by a
force majeure on account of the COVID-19
pandemic has been reached under the Impugned
Order without undertaking any analysis or setting
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 452 of 2022 Page 9 of 34

out any reasoning. To such extent, the Impugned
Order has been rendered indefensible &
unsustainable in light of the settled legal principles.
B. OBTL's prayer for and arbitrary blanket extension of
8 months in terms of the MOP notifications dated
27.07.2020 & 12.06.2021 has been rejected under
the Impugned Order by holding that the same do not
apply in the present case. Further, the Impugned
Order holds that the question as to whether force
majeure has occurred in particular case or not will
be decided by the Ld. UPERC on a case-to-case
basis considering scope of project, extent, duration
of impact, its effects, etc. However, the Impugned
Order fails to take such findings to their logical
sequitur as such analysis is conspicuous by its
absence under the Impugned Order.
C. In granting an extension in SCOD of 160 days qua
Element 1 & 146 days qua Elements 2 to 8 of LOT-
1 of the Project, the Impugned Order fails justify the
grant of such extension on a "day for day basis" as
mandated by Article 4.4.2 of the TSA. To such
extent, the Impugned Order rendered by Ld.
UEPRC is contrary to the TSA provisions.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 452 of 2022 Page 10 of 34

D. By way of its notice dated 21.09.2020, issued in
purported compliance of Article 6.1.1 of the TSA,
OBTL intimated 21.11.2020 as the firm & fixed date
on which Elements 1 to 8 of LOT-1 of its Project
would achieve COD. In effect, OBTL admitted and
conceded that the construction of the aforesaid
elements was not affected/hindered in any manner.
Therefore, applying the principles of law settled by
the Hon'ble Supreme Court in a catena of
judgments including, Energy Watchdog v. CERC
& Ors. reported as (2017)14 SCC 80, no force
majeure event occurred insofar as construction of
Elements 1 to 8 of OBTL's Project is concerned.
E. Instead of appreciating its true meaning, import and
effect, the Impugned Order inexplicably classifies
OBTL's notice dated 21.09.2020 as a force majeure
mitigation step covered by Article 11.6 of the TSA.
F. Having taken cognizance of the fact that the State
Transmission Utility i.e. Nominee of LTTC's had
already granted 3 months extension for
transmission projects under construction as of
25.03.2020 on account of the COVID-19 pandemic,
the Impugned Order is unjustified in granting an
extension of 160 days qua Element 1 & 146 days
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 452 of 2022 Page 11 of 34

qua Elements 2 to 8 without any analysis or
justification to substantiate such divergence.
G. Having inter alia held under its order dated
03.06.2022 that the presence of UPPTCL, being the
STU & nominee of lead LTTCs during the
construction period, was of utmost necessity for
adjudication of Petition No. 1824/2022, the
Impugned Order issued in complete ignorance of
UPPTCL's only effective pleading (i.e., application
for re-hearing) is unsustainable.”
13. We have heard Mr. Abhishek Kumar, Learned Counsel for the
Appellant and Mr. Sourav Roy, Learned Counsel for the 1st
Respondent. We have also perused the written submissions filed by
the Learned Counsels.
14. Learned Counsel for the Appellants strenuously argued that
despite holding the notification dated 27th July, 2020 and 12th June,
2021 issued by Ministry of power, Government of India are
inapplicable to the intra-sate transmission project in question of 1st
Respondent and that the occurrence of Force Majeure has to be
examined on case to case basis considering the scope of project,
extent, duration of impact, its effects, etc., the Commission has failed
to take its own findings to their logical sequitur by failing to do any
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 452 of 2022 Page 12 of 34

such analysis. It is submitted that without any detailed analysis with
regards to the scope of the project, extent and duration of the impact
of Covid-19 Pandemic upon it, the Commission has concluded in one
single paragraph that delay in achieving COD of the elements 1 to 8
was due to Covid-19 Pandemic and deserved to be condoned.
15. Learned Counsel would argue that these findings of the
Commission are contrary to the Articles 4 & 4.2 of the TSA which
provides that any extension ought to be granted on a day for day
basis. It is also argued by the Learned Counsel that the Commission
has failed to take notice of the order dated 24th March, 2020 issued
by Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India exempting the
power transmission licensees from lockdown and subsequent order
dated 16th April, 2020 exempting erection of power transmission lines
from lockdown. It is pointed out to the Learned Counsel that 2nd
Respondent – UPPTCL had granted an extension of three months on
account of Covid-19 Pandemic but no analysis has been done in the
impugned order as to why such three months extension was
insufficient for completing of the project of 1st Respondent
necessitating extension of 160 days for Element I and 146 days for
Element 2 to 8.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 452 of 2022 Page 13 of 34

16. Learned Counsel also referred to the letter dated 21st
September, 2020 issued by the 1st Respondent intimating that the
Elements 1 to 8 of the project would be ready for SCOD i.e. 21st
November, 2020. It is his submission that this letter is a categorical
admission on the part of the 1st Respondent that its performance was
not affected by any Force Majeure event and therefore, claim for
extension of SCOD ought to have been rejected on the basis of the
said letter.
17. Per contra, it is argued on the behalf of Learned Counsel for
Respondent No. 1 that the Commission has considered all the
relevant facts and documents while recognizing Covid-19 Pandemic
as a Force Majeure event under Article 11 of the TSA, and has
lawfully extended SCOD of LOT-1 in terms of Article 4 & 4.1 of the
TSA. It is submitted that the Commission rightly found that the
Respondent No. 1 has served proper notices on the Appellants under
Article 11.5 of TSA informing them about the outbreak/spread out
Covid-19 Pandemic amounted to Force Majeure events. It is also
submitted that the letter dated 21st September, 2020 issued by 1st
Respondent merely reflected the bonafide efforts of 1st Respondent
to mitigate the impact of Covid-10 Pandemic and to endeavor to meet
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 452 of 2022 Page 14 of 34

the SCOD. It does not constitute waiver or abandonment of the
previously issued Force Majeure notices and must be read with the
subsequent Force Majeure notice dated 23rd October, 2020 issued
by 1st Respondent to LTTCs again citing Force Majeure as a reason
for delay in achieving SCOD.
18. Learned Counsel for the 1st Respondent would further argue
that the grant of three months extension from 21st November, 2020 to
21st February, 2021 by the Appellants themselves indicates that they
have accepted that the project was affected by Force Majeure events
post 21st September, 2020. The reliance is placed upon the
judgement of Hon’ble Supreme Court in Mumbai International Airport
(P) Ltd. Vs. Golden Chariot Airport, (2010) 10 SCC 422 canvassed
that a party to any legal proceedings cannot be permitted to raise
contradictory pleas. Learned Counsel would further argue that by not
objecting to any Force Majeure notice issued by 1st Respondent, the
Appellants shall be taken to have accepted all the notices and,
therefore, were precluded from objecting to the claim of 1st
Respondent before the Commission. On these submissions, Learned
Counsel sought dismissal of the appeal .
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 452 of 2022 Page 15 of 34

Our Analysis
19. We find that discussion of the Commission on the issue
“outbreak of Covid-19 Pandemic as Force Majeure event” is in the
paragraph Nos. 99 to 102 of the impugned order which are extracted
hereinbelow:-
“99. The Petitioner vide notice dated 26.03.2020 issued
notice to UPPTCL and LTTCs regarding force majeure on
account of outbreak of Covid-19 in the Country. It was
informed that as a precautionary measure to restrict the
spread of Covid-19, national wide lockdown was imposed
for 21 days effective from 25.03.2020. Due to imposition
of lockdown and restriction in movement, the Petitioner
faced issues related to non-availability of goods and
material, disruption of supply and execution schedule,
administrative support from the Government,
transportation and accessibility issues, delay in
compensation payment to landowners, availability of
manpower, unworkable condition etc. Subsequently,
various notices vide dated 15.04.2020, 04.05.2020,
18.05.2020, 06.06.2020, 04.07.2020, 20.08.2020, 14.09
2020, 23.10.2020 and 29.04.2020 were sent to LTTC's to
update them regarding the current situation with respect
to Covid-19 and how the same affect the Petitioner in
completion the project. Petitioner's activities of
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 452 of 2022 Page 16 of 34

transmission line came to halt with effect from
25.03.2020.
100. At the outset, it would be prudent to first examine
advance notice dated 21.09.2020 regarding
charging/commissioning of elements, before getting into
the merits of relief claimed under force majeure on
account of Covid-19 pandemic, as it has been argued by
the Respondents that since Petitioner has issued notice
dated 21.09.2020 stating that LOT-1 would be ready by
Scheduled SCOD therefore, all the force majeure notices
prior to notice dated 21.09.2020, get blurred out and are
irrelevant in view of Petitioner's categorical admission
under the said letter.
On perusal of records, the Commission noted that notice
dated 21.09.2020 provides that LOT-1 having eight
elements would be ready for charging/ commissioning by
21.11.2020. It is pertinent to mention that the Petitioner
was affected by the force majeure event on account of
Covid-19 which could not be denied as then prevailing
situation was known to everyone. However, Petitioner in
terms of Article 11.6 of the TSA was duty bound to
perform and mitigate the effects of any event of force
majeure as soon as practical. Therefore, it can be agreed
that Petitioner was trying to fulfil its obligation to
commission the project on time considering its duty to
perform under the TSA to mitigate the effect of any event
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 452 of 2022 Page 17 of 34

of force majeure while using its reasonable efforts.
Therefore, the argument of the Respondents regarding
non acceptance of all the force majeure notices prior to
notice dated 21.09.2020 cannot be agreed as the
Petitioner has made reasonable efforts in trying to
commission the project on time, which ultimately got
delayed due to continued effects of pandemic.
101. While coming on merits, it is pertinent to mention
that National Disaster Management Authority issued
order dated 24.03.2020 directing Ministries/ Departments
of Government of India (GOI), State Governments and
State Authorities to take measures to prevent the spread
of Covid-19 in the country. In pursuant to the same,
Ministry of Home Affairs issued order dated 24.03.2020
and various subsequent guidelines from time to time for
their strict implementation. The Government of Uttar
Pradesh also issued guidelines from time to time.
102. The Commission has observed that the Petitioner
from time to time has issued various force majeure notices
to LTTCs and UPPTCL intimating about the force majeure
on account of outbreak of Covid-19 pandemic. UPPCL
vide letter dated 10.08.2020 denied force majeure notice
dated 04.07.2020 by stating that the GOI made it clear
that construction activities including laying/ erecting
power transmission line were allowed during the period of
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 452 of 2022 Page 18 of 34

lockdown subject to proper precaution and social
distancing measures being followed. However, GOI and
various authorities have allowed the extension of SCOD
on account of Covid-19 pandemic like MOP vide
notification dated 27.07.2020 have allowed five months
extension to all inter-state transmission projects which
were under construction as on date of lockdown i.e.
25.03.2020. Further, MOP vide notification dated
12.06.2021 gave another three months, extension to the
inter-state transmission projects which are under
construction with SCOD coming after 01.04.2021. Also,
MNRE vide Office Memorandum dated 17.04.2020 has
also treated Covid-19 as a force majeure event and
considered similar extension of time in SCOD. Further, in
view of the extraordinary circumstances which prevailed
due to Covid-19, nationwide lockdown and in compliance
of order dated 30.05.2020 of Ministry of Home Affairs,
UPPTCL gave three months time extension to its turnkey
projects/ supply contracts/ work contracts in force on
25.03.2020 with provision to consider relaxation on case-
to-case basis/ as a whole depending on the situation in
future. As stated in letter dated 07.12.2021 of UPPCL,
LTTCs in the instant case has also allowed extension of
three months in SCOD of the LOT-1.”
20. Perusal of the above quoted portion of the impugned order of
the Commission would reveal that the Commission has taken note of
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 452 of 2022 Page 19 of 34

the rival submission of the parties, Force Majeure notices issued by
the 1st Respondent to the Appellants, the applicability of notification
dated 23rd July, 2020 and 12th June, 2021, issued by Ministry of
Power, Govt. of India and the O.M. dated 17th April, 2020 issued by
Ministry of Renewable Energy (MNRE) Govt. of India as well as the
three months time extension granted by UPPTCL itself to its turn key
projects, supply contracts, work contracts in force on 25th March,
2020 in view of nationwide lock down to Covid-19 Pandemic and
accordingly came to conclusion that the 1st Respondent is entitled to
seek extension of SCOD on account of Covid-19 Pandemic.
21. Therefore, the submissions made on behalf of the Appellants
that the Commission has concluded in just one single paragraph that
the delay in achieving COD of the Elements 1 to 8 was on account of
Covid-19 Pandemic without any detailed analysis, cannot be
countenanced and are liable to be rejected forthwith. Manifestly, the
Commission has analyzed in detail the submissions of the parties on
this aspect as well as relevant material on record before reaching the
conclusion that delay in achieving SCOD of Element 1 to 8 of LOT-1
of the project by the 1st Respondent was due to Covid-19 Pandemic.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 452 of 2022 Page 20 of 34

22. Further, we may note that Article 4.4. of the TSA executed
between the parties provides for extension of time and is extracted
hereinbelow :-
“4.4 Extension of time:
4.4.1 In the event that the TSP is prevented from
performing its obligations under Article 4.1(a), (b)
and (e) by the stipulated date, due to any Long Term
Transmission Customers' Event of Default, the
Scheduled COD shall be extended, by a 'day for
day' basis, subject to the provisions of Article 13.
4.4.2 In the event that an Element or the Project cannot
be commissioned by its Scheduled COD on account
of any Force Majeure Event as per Article 11, the
Scheduled COD shall be extended, by a 'day for
day' basis, for a maximum period of one hundred
and eighty (180) days. In case the Force Majeure
Event continues even after the maximum period of
one hundred and eighty (180) days, the TSP or the
Majority Long Term Transmission Customers may
choose to terminate the Agreement as per the
provisions of Article 13.5.
4.4.3 If the Parties have not agreed, within thirty (30) days
after the affected Party's performance has ceased
to be affected by the relevant circumstance, on how
long the Scheduled COD should be deferred by, any
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 452 of 2022 Page 21 of 34

Party may raise the Dispute to be resolved in
accordance with Article 16.”
23. Article 4.4.2 is relevant for our consideration which provides
that in case an Element or the project cannot be commissioned by
the SCOD on account of Force Majeure event envisaged under
Article 11, the SCOD shall be extended for a maximum period of 180
days and in case the Force Majeure event continues even after the
said period of 180 days, the transmission service provider or the
majority of LTTCs may refuse to terminate the agreement.
24. Article 11 of the TSA specifies the Force Majeure events and
the consequences thereof. The same is reproduced hereinbelow :-
“ARTICLE : 11
11 FORCE MAJEURE
11.1 Definitions
11.1.1 The following terms shall have the meanings
given hereunder.
11.2 Affected Party
11.2.1 An Affected Party means any of the Long Term
Transmission Customers or the TSP whose
performance has been affected by an event of
Force Majeure.
11.2.2 An event of Force Majeure affecting the CTU/STU
or any agent of the Long Term Transmission
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 452 of 2022 Page 22 of 34

Customers, which has affected the
Interconnection Facilities, shall be deemed to be
an event of Force Majeure affecting the Long
Term Transmission Customers.
11.2.3 Any event of Force Majeure shall be deemed to
be an event of Force Majeure affecting the TSP
only if the Force Majeure event affects and results
in, late delivery of machinery and equipment for
the Project or construction, completion,
commissioning of the Project by Scheduled COD
and/or operation thereafter;
11.3 Force Majeure
A 'Force Majeure' means any event or
circumstance or combination of events and
circumstances including those stated below that
wholly or partly prevents or unavoidably delays an
Affected Party in the performance of its
obligations under this Agreement, but only if and
to the extent that such events or circumstances
are not within the reasonable control, directly or
indirectly, of the Affected Party and could not have
been avoided if the Affected Party had taken
reasonable care or complied with Prudent Utility
Practices:
(a) Natural Force Majeure Events:
act of God, including, but not limited to drought,
fire and explosion (to the extent originating from
a source external to the Site), earthquake,
volcanic eruption, landslide, flood, cyclone,
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 452 of 2022 Page 23 of 34

typhoon, tornado, or exceptionally adverse
weather conditions which are in excess of the
statistical measures for the last hundred (100)
years.
(b) Non-Natural Force Majeure Events:
i. Direct Non-Natural Force Majeure Events
• Nationalization or compulsory
acquisition by any Indian Governmental
Instrumentality of any material assets or
rights of the TSP; or
• the unlawful, unreasonable or
discriminatory revocation of, or refusal
to renew, any Consents, Clearances
and Permits required by the TSP to
perform their obligations under the RFP
Project Documents or any unlawful,
unreasonable or discriminatory refusal
to grant any other Consents,
Clearances and Permits required for the
development/ operation of the Project,
provided that a Competent Court of Law
declares the revocation or refusal to be
unlawful, unreasonable and
discriminatory and strikes the same
down; or
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 452 of 2022 Page 24 of 34

• any other unlawful, unreasonable or
discriminatory action on the part of an
Indian Governmental Instrumentality
which is directed against the Project,
provided that a Competent Court of Law
declares the action to be unlawful,
unreasonable and discriminatory and
strikes the same down.
ii. Indirect Non - Natural Force Majeure
Events
• act of war (whether declared or
undeclared), invasion, armed conflict
or act of foreign enemy, blockade,
embargo, revolution, riot,
insurrection, terrorist or military
action; or
• radioactive contamination or ionising
radiation originating from a source in
India or resulting from any other
Indirect Non Natural Force Majeure
Event mentioned above, excluding
circumstances where the source or
cause of contamination or radiation
is brought or has been brought into
or near the Site by the Affected Party
or those employed or engaged by
the Affected Party; or
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 452 of 2022 Page 25 of 34

• industry wide strikes and labour
disturbances, having a nationwide
impact in India/statewide impact in
Uttar Pradesh.
11.4 Force Majeure Exclusions
11.4.1 Force Majeure shall not include (i) any event or
circumstance which is within the reasonable
control of the Parties and (ii) the following
conditions, except to the extent that they are
consequences of an event of Force Majeure:
(a) Unavailability, late delivery, or changes in cost of
the machinery, equipment, materials, spare parts
etc. for the Project;
(b) Delay in the performance of any Contractors or
their agents;
(c) Non-performance resulting from normal wear and
tear typically experienced in transmission
materials and equipment;
(d) Strikes or labour disturbance at the facilities of the
Affected Party;
(e) Insufficiency of finances or funds or the
Agreement becoming onerous to perform; and
(f) Non-performance caused by, or connected with,
the Affected Party's:
i. negligent or intentional acts, errors or
omissions;
ii. failure to comply with an Indian Law; or
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 452 of 2022 Page 26 of 34

iii. breach of, or default under this Agreement
or any Project Documents.”
25. Undisputedly, there is no specific reference to a pandemic as
a Force Majeure event under Article 11.3. Understandably so,
since the last pandemic of comparable magnitude, the Spanish
Flu of 1918–1920, had occurred nearly a century earlier. Given
the remarkable advances in medical science since then, no one
could have anticipated that a pandemic of such magnitude could
once again strike the world, with devastating consequences,
bringing normal life and economic activity across the globe to a
virtual standstill. COVID-19 was a catastrophe of immense
magnitude, spreading across the globe and disrupting not only
the normal course of daily life but also adversely affecting the
mental health of people and the economies of nations. It caused
severe social and economic disruption worldwide, resulting in
over seven million confirmed deaths globally. A careful perusal
of the first paragraph of Article 11.3 makes it clear that COVID-
19 satisfies the attributes prescribed therein for an event to
qualify as a Force Majeure Event. This is particularly so since
COVID-19 does not fall within any of the exclusions specified in
Article 11.4.1. However, while a pandemic like COVID-19 is
closest in nature and origin to the events described in Article
11.3(a), relating to Natural Force Majeure Events, its
consequences, particularly the disruption of work and
movement of goods and personnel pursuant to governmental
orders issued to contain the pandemic, bear a closer
resemblance to the events contemplated under Article 11.3(b),
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 452 of 2022 Page 27 of 34

relating to Non-Natural Force Majeure Events. A close
examination of the TSA, however, reveals that the distinction
between Natural and Non-Natural Force Majeure Events is not
material for deciding the issue in the present appeal.
26. Covid-19 Pandemic has already been recognized as Force
Majeure event by the Govt. of India, MNRE as well as UPPTCL itself
by granting extensions to the transmission project which were under
construction as on date of lockdown i.e. dated 25th March, 2020. It is
true that the notifications dated 27th July, 2020 and 12th June, 2021
issued by Ministry of power granting 5 months extension to the
transmission projects were applicable to inter-state transmission
projects only but that cannot be taken to indicate that Covid-19
Pandemic was not a Force Majeure event in respect of intra-state
transmission projects. Even otherwise also, the Appellants have not
contested that fact that Covid-19 Pandemic was a Force Majeure
event. Their only contention is that the 1st Respondent was not
entitled to the extension of the SCOD of its project as its progress was
not hampered in any manner by the Covid-19 Pandemic.
27. The Appellants have not disputed the fact that 1st Respondent
has issued various Force Majeure notices dated 20th February, 2020,
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 452 of 2022 Page 28 of 34

23rd March, 2020, 26th March, 2020, 15th April, 2020, 29th April, 2020,
4th May, 2020, 18th May, 2020, 6th June, 2020, 4th July, 2020, 20th
August, 2020, 14th September, 2020 and 23rd October, 2020
intimating them about the impact of Covid-19 Pandemic upon the
progress of the project and seeking extension of SCOD of the project
as per Article 4.4 of the TSA. Concededly, none of the notice has
been responded to by the Appellants. The Appellants maintained
stoic silence on these notices in which claim for extension of SCOD
of the project was made by the 1st Respondent specifically. Therefore,
the Appellants shall be presumed to have accepted the fact that the
project of the 1st Respondent got impacted by the Covid-19
Pandemic.
28. Relying upon the communication dated 21st September, 2020
issued by the 1st Respondent to Appellants, intimating that the project
would be ready for commissioning by the 21st November, 2020, it is
argued on behalf of the Appellants that there was a categorical
admission on behalf of the 1st Respondent that this project was not in
any way affected by the Force Majeure event, and, therefore, the
claim for extension of SCOD ought to have been rejected. We do not
find any force in the submission on behalf of the Appellants. Perusal
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 452 of 2022 Page 29 of 34

of the communication dated 21st September, 2020 does reveal that
the 1st Respondent had notified the Appellants that the project would
be ready for charging and commissioning by 21st November, 2020.
However, the contents of the said communication need to be read
juxtaposition with subsequent Force Majeure notice dated 23rd
October, 2020 issued by the 1st Respondent, as argued by the
learned Counsel for the 1st Respondent. In the said subsequent
notice, the 1st Respondent has referred to the order dated 30th
September, 2020 issued by the Union Home Secretary, thereby
extending the lockdown in containment zones upto 31st October,
2020. It has further been stated in the said notice that in view of the
said order of the Government, the 1st Respondent is facing following
issues :-
• “Movement of gangs has been affected since transportation of
labours in groups is limited and hence causing delay in getting
required no. of labours at site in timely manner. Due to
suspension of railway services, interstate movement of gangs
has been affected.
• Administrative support from the Government are still very
limited. Also, due to identification of containment zones, few of
the Collector offices have limited staff & closed majority of
times.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 452 of 2022 Page 30 of 34

• Accessibility to landowners for resolving ROW issues for
various locations is getting affected due to fear in villagers for
Covid-19 spread & so they show resistance for meeting &
thereby clearance of ROW.
• Delay in compensation payment to landowners due to limited
staff available in banks which results in prolongation for
issuance of Demand Drafts, which delays construction
activities.
• Availability of manpower to achieve the desired output of the
contract works.
• Processing of Statutory proposals like NH, Forest clearance
as these are not moving as per desired pace.
• Liasoning part for applying shutdowns (various crossings like
Power line/Railways/NHAI) affected.
• Due to identification of Containment zones, few of our site
offices were also closed as per instructions from
administration.”
29. The 1st Respondent has further sated in the said notice that
despite being affected by the Force Majeure event, they are making
best efforts to mitigate the effects of Force Majeure and are making
endeavour to complete the project by the SCOD. Accordingly, the
request for grant of extension of COD was reiterated in the said
notice.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 452 of 2022 Page 31 of 34

30. What is relevant to note is that the order dated 30th September,
2020 issued by Union Home Secretary along with the guidelines was
post the notice dated 21st September, 2020 issued by 1st Respondent
to the Appellants and, therefore, once the 1st Respondent realized
that the progress of the project would get further impacted in view of
the restrictions placed by virtue of order dated 30th September, 2020
of the Union Home Secretary, it immediately intimated the Appellants
about the same vide notice dated 23rd October, 2020 as detailed
hereinabove. Therefore, in these circumstances, it would be totally
incorrect and unjust to accept that in view of the contents of the
communication dated 21st September 2020 issued to the 1st
Respondent, performance of its project was not affected by any Force
Majeure event.
31. Letter dated 7th December, 2021 addressed by UPPCL to
Superintendent Engineer (Electricity), Import-Export & Payment
Circle, Lucknow, with a copy to the 1st Respondent, is also pertinent
on this aspect and needs to be taken note of. Vide the said letter,
UPPCL has itself granted three months extension of SCOD to the
Elements 1 to 8 of LOT-I of the project of 1st Respondent i.e. from
21st November, 2020 to 21st February, 2021. Apparently, the
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 452 of 2022 Page 32 of 34

extension has been granted on account of the impact of Covid-19
Pandemic on the progress of transmission projects, even though, it is
not said so specifically in the same. Nothing has been brought on
record on behalf of the Appellants to contend otherwise. Therefore,
once the UPPCL itself acknowledged the Covid-19 Pandemic as
Force Majeure event and granted extension of three months, SCOD
of the project itself, the Appellants cannot be heard to contend that
the Commission committed any error or illegality in holding the 1st
Respondent entitled to extension of COD of its project on account of
Covid-19 Pandemic.
32. What comes out of the above analysis is that the 1st
Respondent has regularly been apprising the Appellants about the
occurrence of Force Majeure event (i.e. Covid-19 Pandemic) right
since 20th February, 2020 (date of first Force Majeure notice) till 23rd
October, 2020 (last Force Majeure notice) with the request for
extension of SCOD of the project under Act 4.4. of the TSA. The
Appellants chose not to respond to any of these notices and
maintained stoic silence. Covid-19 Pandemic, as a Force Majeure
event, falls in Article 11.3(b)(ii) of the TSA. There is nothing on record
to suggest that the project of the Appellant was not delayed or in any
manner impacted by Covid-19 Pandemic. Ministry of power, Govt. of
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Appeal No. 452 of 2022 Page 33 of 34

India, has vide notifications dated 25th March, 2020 and 12th
February, 2021 granted 5 months extension to the inter-state
transmission projects, the benefit of which must enure to the intra-
state transmission projects too. UPPCL (i.e. Appellant No. 1) itself
granted three months extension of SCOD to the project of 1st
Respondent vide letter dated 07.12.2021 on account of Covid-19
Pandemic. Considering all these facts and circumstances, we are
unable to fathom that the Commission has erred in passing the
impugned order.
Conclusion
33. Having regard to the above discussion, we are not able to find
any error or infirmity in the impugned order of the Commission. The
appeal is devoid of any merit and is hereby dismissed accordingly.
All pending IAs shall also stand disposed of.
Pronounced in the open court on this 29th day of September, 2026.
Ajay Talegaonkar Virender Bhat
Technical Member (Electricity) Judicial Member

items.pdf_text:
Court-2
IN THE APPELLATE TRIBUNAL FOR ELECTRICITY
(Appellate Jurisdiction)
APPEAL NO.329 OF 2017
Dated: 29.09.2026
Present: Hon`ble Mr. Virender Bhat, Judicial Member
Hon`ble Mr. Ajay Talegaonkar, Technical Member
In the matter of:
M/s Radiant Solar Energies Pvt. Ltd.
Through its Director (Saurabh Singla)
Muktsar-Faridkot Bye Pass,
KotKapura, District Faridkot,
Punjab – 151204 … Appellant
Versus
1. Punjab State Electricity Regulatory Commission
Through its Secretary
SCO 220-221, Sector 34-A,
Chandigarh-160022
2. Punjab Energy Development Agency
Through its Chief Executive Officer
Plot No. 1 & 2, Sector 33,
Chandigarh - 160020
3. Punjab State Power Corporation Ltd.
Through its Managing Director
The Mall, Patiala – 147001
4. Punjab State Transmission Corporation Ltd.
Through its Managing Director
The Mall, Patiala - 147001 … Respondent (s)
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.329 of 2017 Page 1 of 19

Counsel on record for the Appellant(s) : Tajender K. Joshi
for App. 1
Counsel on record for the Respondent(s): Sakesh Kumar
for Res. 1
Aadil Singh Boparai
for Res. 2
Anand K. Ganesan
Swapna Seshadri
for Res. 3
O R D E R
PER HON’BLE MR. VIRENDER BHAT, JUDICIAL MEMBER
1. The appellant, a solar power generator in the State of Punjab, is
aggrieved by the order dated 09.08.2017 passed by 1st respondent Punjab
State Electricity Regulatory Commission (hereinafter referred to as “the
Commission”) in appellant’s petition no.15/2016 whereby the claim of the
appellant for extension of Scheduled Commercial Operation Date (SCOD) of
its 3MW solar power project on account of force majeure events affecting
the completion/commissioning of the project, has been partly allowed and at
the same time the tariff of 2MW capacity of the plant has been reduced from
Rs.7.58/kWh to Rs.5.09/kWh. The appellant has also been held liable to pay
liquidated damages to 3rd respondent Punjab State Power Corporation
Limited (in short PSPCL) and the bank guarantees given to it by 2nd
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.329 of 2017 Page 2 of 19

respondent Punjab Energy Development Agency (in short PEDA) have been
ordered to be encashed.
2. The 2nd respondent PEDA is a designated nodal agency for
development of renewable energy products in the State of Punjab and is
responsible for promotion as well as development of non-conventional and
renewable sources of energy in the State including solar, mini-hydro,
biomass/agro-based power projects.
3. The 3rd respondent PSPCL is a distribution licensee in the State of
Punjab and the successor in interest of Punjab State Electricity Board after
its unbundling along with Punjab State Transmission Corporation Limited,
which is the respondent no.4.
4. The brief facts, relevant for disposal of the instant appeal, are as
under:-
(i) In the year 2015, 2nd respondent PEDA had invited the private
developers/companies for establishment of an aggregate 250
MW capacity solar projects in the State of Punjab and had issued
a Request for Proposal (RFP) document in this regard. The
capacity to be developed was divided into three categories i.e.
Category-I projects of 1-4 MW capacity (aggregate capacity
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.329 of 2017 Page 3 of 19

50MW), Category-II projects 5-24 MW (aggregate capacity
100MW) and Category-III projects 25-50 MW (aggregate
capacity 100MW). The power to be generated from these
projects was to be sold to third respondent PSPCL for a period
of 25 years for supply to the consumers in the State of Punjab.
(ii) The selection of bidders was based on net availed tariff after
providing discount on generic tariff notified by the Commission
for solar PV power projects for Financial Year (FY) 2014-15
irrespective of availing normal rate of depreciation/accelerated
rate of depreciation.
(iii) The Commission determined generic levelized generation tariff
for renewable energy power projects for FY 2014-15 vide order
dated 05.09.2014 in petition no.42/2014 (suo moto) wherein the
generic tariff for solar power projects was fixed at Rs.7.72/kWh.
(iv) The appellant had submitted its bid for 3MW project under
Category-I. Based on the bids received from the bidders, PEDA
allocated a total capacity of 229MW solar PV power projects to
various developers under different categories. The appellant
was allotted 3MW solar PV power project vide Letter of Award
(LoA) dated 25.02.2015. As per the provisions of RFP, the
appellant was required to supply power to the 3rd respondent
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.329 of 2017 Page 4 of 19

PSPCL from its power project for a period of 25 years at a net
tariff of Rs.7.58/kWh upon providing a discount on the generic
tariff of Rs.7.72/kWh as notified by the Commission in its RE tariff
order dated 05.09.2014.
(v) The appellant signed the Implementation Agreement (IA) as well
as Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) for setting up of the project
with PEDA and PSPCL on 19.03.2015 and 31.03.2015
respectively. As per the provisions of the PPA, the project was
required to be commissioned within 10 months from the date of
signing of the PPA. Thus, the SCOD of the project was
31.01.2016. The PPA was approved by the Commission vide
order dated 11.05.2015.
(vi) Meanwhile, the appellant had applied for grid technical feasibility
clearance on 23.04.2015 which was granted by PSPCL on
27.05.2015.
(vii) The appellant was unable to commission the project by its SCOD
i.e. 31.01.2016, purportedly on account of some force majeure
events. Ultimately, the 1MW capacity of the plant was
commissioned on 18.05.2016 and the remaining 2MW capacity
was commissioned on 15.03.2017.
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.329 of 2017 Page 5 of 19

(viii) Since the appellant apprehended that PSPCL may initiate action
in terms of Clause 10.1.0 of PPA and Article 7.0 A of IA i.e.
forfeiture of Performance Bank Guarantee, it approached the
Commission by way of petition no.15/2016 claiming following
reliefs: -
“a) direct PSPCL and PSTCL to make the bay ready for
synchronization;
b) restrain respondents from forfeiture of performance
bank guarantees in terms of clause 10.1.0 of PPA
and article 7.0 A of IA till bay is ready for
synchronization;
c) extend the date of commissioning of the project till
bay is ready for synchronization.”
(ix) Prayers (a) and (b) had been made in the petition as, according
to the appellant, PSPCL was unable to complete the construction
of 66kV bay at Pathrala sub-station even after nine months of
granting grid feasibility clearance to the appellant and had also
failed to install potential transformers as well as other electrical
equipment.
(x) The petition has been disposed of by the Commission vide
impugned order dated 09.08.2017 thereby condoning the delay
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.329 of 2017 Page 6 of 19

of 49 days (41 days from the date of signing of PPA on
31.03.2015 up to date of its approval by the Commission i.e.
11.05.2015 plus 8 days from 10.05.2016 when the appellant
applied for synchronization of the project to the grid till
18.05.2016 when the 1MW capacity of the project was
commissioned). The Commission has refused to condone the
remaining part of delay in commissioning of the 1MW capacity as
well as 2 MW capacity of the project as sought by the appellant.
While keeping the tariff of 1MW capacity undisturbed, the
Commission worked out the tariff of 2MW capacity at
Rs.5.09/kWh.
(xi) Accordingly, the appellant is before us in this appeal.
5. We have heard Shri Tajender K. Joshi, learned counsel for the
appellant Shri Sakesh Kumar, learned counsel for the 1st respondent
Commission, Shri Adil Singh Boparai, learned counsel for the 2nd respondent
PEDA and Mr. Anand Ganesan, learned counsel for the 3rd respondent
PSPCL. We have also perused the written submissions filed on behalf of
appellant, 2nd respondent and the 3rd respondent. The Commission has not
filed written submissions.
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.329 of 2017 Page 7 of 19

Our Analysis: -
6. In the Memo of Appeal, it has been the contention of the appellant that:
(i) The entire delay in commissioning of the project ought to
have been condoned and SCOD of the entire project ought
to have been extended in view of the force majeure events
agitated by the appellant; and
(ii) the tariff of said 2Mw capacity of the project ought not to have
been reduced to a tariff arrived in the subsequent year for a
50MW capacity project.
7. During the hearing of the appeal, the learned counsel for the appellant
did not advance any submissions on point no.(i) hereinabove and confined
his submissions only to point no.(ii) hereinabove. His submission was that
this Tribunal may consider the point no.(i) and decide the same as per its
wisdom.
8. We may note that with regards to 1MW capacity of the power project,
the Commission has returned the following findings in the impugned order:-
“The Commission notes that as per the PPA, the SCOD of the
project was 30.01.2016. The 1 MW capacity of the project was
commissioned on 18.05.2016 after a delay of 109 days.
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.329 of 2017 Page 8 of 19

However, though the said capacity of the project at site was
ready for synchronization on 09.04.2016, the work of 66 kV line
was completed by the petitioner on 03.05.2016. The petitioner
applied for synchronization clearance on 10.05.2016 and the
same was granted by PSPCL on the same date. However, the
1 MW capacity of the project was commissioned on
18.05.2016 as the work of the 66 kV bay at Pathrala sub-
station was completed by PSPCL on 17.05.2016. As such, the
delay in commissioning of the 1 MW capacity of the project
from 30.01.2016 to 10.05.2016 (101 days) is attributable to the
petitioner and from 10.05.2016 to 18.05.2016 (8 days) is
attributable to PSPCL. The Commission has already allowed
above the period of 41 days in favour of the petitioner. Thus, a
total period of 49(41+8) days is allowable to the benefit of the
petitioner. Therefore, the commissioning of 1 MW capacity of
the project is considered to be delayed by the petitioner by 60
(109-49) days and the same is deemed to have been
commissioned on 30.03.2016 which is within the validity of the
applicable tariff i.e. 31.03.2016.
Thus, the petitioner is liable for forfeiture of the PBGs for
the said delay in terms of article 7.0 A (i) of the IA and clause
10.1.0 of the PPA. It is clarified that there is neither any case
for levy of liquidated damages by PSPCL nor any adverse
impact on the tariff mentioned in the PPA with regard to the 1
MW capacity of the project commissioned on 18.05.2016.”
(Emphasis supplied)
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.329 of 2017 Page 9 of 19

9. Having regard to the material on record which has been duly
considered by the Commission while passing the impugned order, we do not
find any ground to interfere in these findings of the Commission.
10. With regards to the balance 2MW capacity of the project, the
Commission has returned following findings in the impugned order: -
“The said 2 MW capacity was commissioned on 15.03.2017.
The petitioner justified the delay stating that SIDBI curtailed
funds due to non completion of 66 KV bay work at Pathrala
sub-station. The petitioner wrote a letter dated 11.07.2016 to
SIDBI to disburse the remaining loan amount. SIDBI vide letter
dated 26.08.2016 informed that it is ready to disburse the
remaining loan amount subject to certain conditions. The
petitioner procured the solar PV modules for the remaining 2
MW capacity on 01.02.2017 and commissioned the same on
15.03.2017. The Commission is not convinced of the
submissions made by the petitioner with regard to delay in
completion of the remaining 2 MW capacity due to delayed
disbursement of loan by SIDBI. The petitioner appears to have
not followed up diligently with SIDBI for releasing the remaining
funds. After commissioning of 1 MW capacity on 18.05.2016,
the petitioner approached SIDBI on11.07.2016 for the purpose
who reverted back on 26.08.2016 and confirmed that it is ready
to disburse the remaining loan and accepted the revised date
of commissioning as 31.03.2017. However, the petitioner did
not take any concrete action to complete the remaining work.
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.329 of 2017 Page 10 of 19

Even otherwise, the petitioner had earlier categorically made
the submissions that the project will be funded through internal
resources/unsecured loans from the parent company. As such,
it is felt that the petitioner had the financial capability to
commission the remaining 2 MW capacity much earlier.
PSPCL's submissions that it was the lackadaisical attitude of
the petitioner which delayed the project appear more
convincing and the Commission tends to agree.
The remaining 2 MW capacity was commissioned on
15.03.2017 i.e. 410 days after the due date of commissioning
on 30.01.2016. Considering the benefit of 49 (41+8) days
allowed by the Commission in favour of the petitioner in the
paras above while working out the delay in commissioning of
1 MW capacity, the net delay attributable to the petitioner in
commissioning of the remaining 2 MW capacity works out to
361 (410-49) days.
Thus, the petitioner is liable for forfeiture of the PBGs by
PEDA, in terms of the provisions in article 7.0 of the IA and
clause 10.1.0 of the PPA in respect of 2 MW capacity of the
project as well.
As regards the levy of liquidated damages (LD charges)
by PSPCL and payment whereof by the petitioner, it is seen
that the petitioner proceeded with the commissioning of the
remaining 2 MW capacity despite the adverse implications with
regard to levy of liquidated damages upto the date of
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.329 of 2017 Page 11 of 19

commissioning as also adverse impact on the tariff having
been clearly brought out in the Commission's interim Order
dated 24.12.2016 while allowing the petitioner to install the
remaining 2 MW capacity. The Commission had allowed the
same citing circumstances mentioned therein in the interest of
all the stakeholders, even though the same was liable for
cancellation in terms of the contractual documents. As the
remaining 2 MW capacity has been commissioned with a delay
of 361 days, PSPCL is entitled to levy and claim liquidated
damages for the said period at the rate provided in clause
10.1.1 of the PPA.”
(Emphasis supplied)
11. We are also unable to find any error in these findings of the
Commission. We have not found any material on record which may convince
us to take a contrary view and thus, affirm these findings of the Commission.
12. In so far as the tariff for 2Mw capacity of the project, the Commission
has determined the same at Rs.5.09/kWh in place of Rs.7.8/kWh for which
the bid of the appellant had been accepted, on the following reasoning: -
“The tariff was valid till 31.03.2016 in terms of the Order of the
Commission dated 11.05.2015 in petition no. 21 of 2015 and
the IA/PPA. As the remaining 2 MW capacity of the project has
been commissioned with a delay of 361 days beyond the
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.329 of 2017 Page 12 of 19

SCOD on 30.01.2016, the tariff of ₹ 7.58 per kWh for the said
capacity would no longer hold good. The Commission has
determined the tariff for the remaining 2 MW capacity of the
project in the following para.
The tariff of ₹ 7.58 per kWh for the petitioner's project was
determined through competitive bidding process undertaken
by PEDA on the basis of discount to be offered by the bidders
on the generic tariff of ₹ 7.72 per kWh determined by the
Commission for FY 2014-15 and the tariff was valid till
31.03.2016. For FY 2015-16 also, PEDA conducted the
competitive bidding process on the same basis of discount to
be offered by the bidders on the generic tariff of ₹ 7.04 per kWh
for FY 2015-16 determined by the Commission wherein the
lowest tariff discovered was ₹ 5.09 per kWh and approved by
the Commission in its Order dated 10.06.2016 in petition no.31
of 2016 and the same was valid upto 31.03.2017. Under the
circumstances, the Commission considers the petitioner's
project akin to such projects. The Commission notes that in
interim order dated 24.12.2016, it allowed the prayer of the
petitioner in the application dated 08.12.2016 to the extent that
it may add the solar PV modules for the remaining 2 MW
capacity and commission the same by 31.03.2017 without
prejudice to the rights of the respondents accruing due to the
aforesaid extension being granted with regard to, encashment
of Performance Bank Guarantee by PEDA, levy of liquidated
damages by PSPCL upto 31.03.2017 and reduction in tariff of
the petitioner's project, which could be the minimum tariff
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.329 of 2017 Page 13 of 19

discovered in the subsequent bidding process and adopted by
the Commission in its Order dated 10.06.2016 in petition no.
31 of 2016 i.e.₹5.09 per kWh, which shall be decided by the
Commission on merits in the final Order in the petition.
Accordingly, the Commission finds it just and fair to fix the tariff
for the 2 MW capacity out of 3 MW total capacity of the project
as ₹5.09 per kWh. As such, the tariff for the project payable by
PSPCL w.e.f. 15.03.2017 would be worked out on the basis of
the weighted average tariff considering the tariff of ₹7.58 per
kWh for 1 MW capacity and ₹5.09 per kWh for the remaining 2
MW capacity. It is clarified that the tariff for the period
18.05.2016 to 14.03.2017 for the 1 MW capacity would be ₹
7.58 per kWh.”
(Emphasis supplied)
13. It not in any dispute that as per Article 3 (C) of the Implementation
Agreement dated 19.03.2015 executed between the appellant and
respondent no.3, in case the COD of the project goes beyond 31.03.2016,
the tariff stated in Article 3(A) therein shall cease to exist and the project
developer would be required to get the tariff redetermined from the
Commission.
14. In the instant case, the appellant has commissioned the 2MW capacity
of its project on 15.03.2017 with a delay of 410 days out of which 49 days
delay has been condoned by the Commission. Notwithstanding the same,
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.329 of 2017 Page 14 of 19

the COD of the said 2MW capacity of the project has crossed the deadline
of 31.03.2016 and therefore, the appellant is not entitled to the PPA tariff of
Rs.7.58/kWh. The tariff for the said capacity of the project was to be
redetermined by the Commission. The Commission has taken note of the
fact that the lowest tariff discovered in the competitive bidding process for
the FY 2015-16 was Rs.5.09/kWh which was approved vide order dated
10.06.2016 in petition no.31/2016 and was valid up to 31.03.2017. Since the
2MW capacity of the appellant’s project was commissioned on 15.03.2017,
the Commission has applied the said lowest discovered tariff of Rs.5.09/kWh
to the same.
15. Learned counsel for the appellant argued that the competitive bidding
conducted in the year 2015-16, in which the lowest tariff of Rs.5.09/kWh was
discovered, was for inviting bids for a minimum capacity of 50MW. He would
submit that the Commission erred in applying the tariff offered for a 50MW
capacity project to the appellant’s project of 3MW capacity for the reason
that the financing capacity, bargaining capacity and transmission lines
related to a 50MW capacity project are totally distinct from those related to a
3MW capacity project.
16. In this regard, we find it apposite to refer to the case of another solar
developer M/s Abundant Energy Pvt. Ltd which was allotted 1MW capacity
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.329 of 2017 Page 15 of 19

project in the same bidding process in which the appellant has been allotted
the 3MW capacity project. In the case of M/s Abundant also, the
Commission did not extend the SCOD of the project while rejecting the force
majeure claims of the developer. Accordingly, the Commission disposed of
the petition no.25/2016 filed by the developer M/s Abundant Energy Pvt. Ltd.
vide order dated 14.02.2017. At the same time, the Commission reworked
the tariff for the power project of the developer M/s Abundant Energy Pvt.
Ltd. to Rs.5.39/kWh to be payable by PSPCL. Subsequently, the review
petition filed by the developer M/s Abundant Energy Pvt. Ltd was allowed by
the Commission vide order dated 21.05.2018 thereby overturning its
previous order dated 14.02.2017 and allowing the force majeure claims of
the developer. Thus, the SCOD of the project was extended and the PPA
tariff of Rs.7.68/kWh was granted. Against the said order dated 21.05.2018
of the Commission, PSPCL approached this Tribunal by way of appeal
no.316/2018 which was allowed by this Tribunal vide judgment dated
28.08.2024 thereby setting aside the review order dated 21.05.2018 and
restoring the previous order dated 14.02.2017 of the Commission. Thus, this
Tribunal affirmed the redetermined tariff of Rs.5.39/kWh in respect of the
developer M/s Abundant Energy Pvt. Ltd. in that case.
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.329 of 2017 Page 16 of 19

17. The appellant has referred to the said case in its written submissions
but has added that such reference may not be construed as acceptance of
the method of redetermination of tariff adopted by the Commission in the
order passed in that case. The 3rd respondent PSPCL has also referred to
the said case in its written submissions but has attempted to distinguish the
same on the ground that the appellant had procured the modules on
01.10.2017 at reduced prices, and therefore, cannot claim tariff comparable
to the project of M/s Abundant Energy Pvt. Ltd which had achieved COD
much earlier i.e. on 24.08.2016. Another distinction between the two cases,
which is highlighted on behalf of PSPCL, is that the tariff for which bid was
submitted by the appellant in this case was 10paisa less than what was bid
by M/s Abundant Energy Pvt. Ltd. and therefore tariff redetermined for M/s
Abundant Energy Pvt. Ltd. cannot be applied to the appellant herein.
18. We concur with the submissions on behalf of the appellant that the
Commission ought not to have applied the lowest discovered tariff of
Rs.5.09/kWh during the competitive bidding process for FY 2015-16 for the
reason that minimum capacity for which bids were invited was 50MW. By no
stretch of imagination can the tariff discovered for a 50MW project be applied
to a 3MW capacity project. In so far as the tariff of Rs.5.39/kWh determined
for the project of M/s Abundant Energy Pvt. Ltd. (as approved by this Tribunal
also in appeal no.316/2018) is concerned, we note that M/s Abundant Energy
____________________________________________________________________________________
Appeal No.329 of 2017 Page 17 of 19

Pvt. Ltd had commissioned the project on 24.08.2016 indicating that the
entire equipment had been purchased and procured by the developer much
prior to the said date. However, in the instant case, the appellant has
commissioned the project on 15.03.2017. Admittedly, the appellant procured
the modules for the solar plant on 01.02.2017. It is the case of the PSPCL
that at that time, the prices of solar modules had reduced substantially.
Despite contending so, PSPCL did not produce any material to show that the
prices of solar modules prevailing prior to 24.08.2016 had reduced
substantially by January, 2017 and if so, by what percentage. Therefore, we
are unable to hold with certainty that there had been any such substantial or
marginal reduction in the prices of solar modules between August, 2016 and
January, 2017.
19. The fact, however, remains that M/s Abundant Energy Pvt. Ltd. had
submitted its bid at the tariff of Rs.7.68/kWh whereas, the appellant had bid
for the tariff of Rs.7.58/kWh i.e. 10 paisa less than the bid tariff submitted by
M/s Abundant Energy Pvt. Ltd. Therefore, it would be just and fair to reduce
10 paisa from the tariff redetermined by the Commission for the project of
M/s Abundant Energy Pvt. Ltd, as affirmed by this Tribunal in appeal
no.316/2018. By doing so, the tariff to be approved for the project of the
appellant would be Rs.5.29/kWh.

Conclusion: -
20. Thus, we uphold the impugned order of the Commission in so far as it
has refused to condone the delay in commissioning of the solar power project
of the appellant beyond 49 days, has held PEDA entitled to encash the
Performance Bank Guarantee of the appellant and has held the appellant
liable to pay liquidated damages to 3rd respondent PSPCL for the delay of
361 days in commissioning of 2MW capacity of the project. However, the
tariff of Rs.5.09/kWh determined by the Commission for the appellant’s
power project in the impugned order cannot be sustained. We hold that the
appellant shall be entitled to the tariff @Rs.5.29/kWh for the power supplied
from its power project to the 3rd respondent PSPCL.
21. The 3rd respondent PSPCL shall pay entire differential in tariff, if any,
to the appellant within four weeks from the date of this judgment positively.
22. The appeal stands partly allowed, albeit in above terms. All pending
IAs, if any, also stand disposed of.
